(46)

We made extensive use of a special case, the adjacent ordering swap mixing Hamiltonians:

HPS,i,{u,v}=HPS,{i,i+1},{u,v}.H_{\mathrm{PS},{i,\{u,v\}}}=H_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,i+1\},\{u,v\}}}\;. (47)

To swap the iith and jjth elements of the ordering regardless of which cities those are, we used the value-independent ordering swap partial mixing Hamiltonian:

HPS,{i,j}=∑{u,v}∈([n]2)HPS,{i,j},{u,v}.H_{\mathrm{PS},\{i,j\}}=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in\binom{[n]}{2}}H_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}. (48)

Of these (n2)\binom{n}{2} partial mixing Hamiltonians, nn are adjacent value-independent ordering swap partial mixing Hamiltonians:

HPS,i=∑𝜾|(ι1,…​ιi−1,ιi+1,ιi,ιi+2,…,ιn)⟩​⟨(ι1,…,ιn)|,\begin{split}H_{\mathrm{PS},i}&=\sum_{\boldsymbol{\iota}}\Ket{\left(\iota_{1},\ldots\iota_{i-1},\iota_{i+1},\iota_{i},\iota_{i+2},\ldots,\iota_{n}\right)}\Bra{\left(\iota_{1},\ldots,\iota_{n}\right)},\end{split} (49)

which swap the iith element with the subsequent one regardless of which cities those are.

These partial mixers can be combined in several ways to form full mixers, of which we explore two types.

Simultaneous ordering swap mixer.  Defining HPS=∑i=1nHPS,iH_{\mathrm{PS}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}H_{\mathrm{PS},i}, we have the “simultaneous ordering swap mixer”:

Usim​-​PS​(β)=e−i​β​HPS.U_{\mathrm{sim}\text{-}\mathrm{PS}}(\beta)=e^{-i\beta H_{\mathrm{PS}}}. (50)

Different subsets and partitions of the partial mixers UPS,{i,j},{u,v}=e−i​HPS,{i,j},{u,v}U_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}=e^{-iH_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}} and different orderings of a partition yield different partitioned ordering swap mixers. The color parity mixers we now defined use the adjacent partial mixer. Other mixers, using more of the (n2)2{\binom{n}{2}}^{2} partial mixers, are possible, as are repeated versions of the following color-parity ordering swap mixer.

Color-parity ordering swap mixer.  Simultaneous ordering swap mixer. To define the ordered partition, we first defined an ordered partition on the set of adjacent partial mixers UPS,i,{u,v}U_{\mathrm{PS},{i,\{u,v\}}} for a fixed tour position ii, where the parts of this partition contains mutually commuting partial mixers. We then partitioned the ii to obtain a full ordered partition. Two partial mixers UPS,i,{u,v}U_{\mathrm{PS},{i,\{u,v\}}} and UPS,i,{u′,v′}U_{\mathrm{PS},{i,\{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}\}}} commute as long as {u,v}∩{u′,v′}=∅\{u,v\}\cap\{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}\}=\emptyset. Partitioning the (n2)\binom{n}{2} pairs of cities into κ\kappa parts such that each part contains only mutually disjoint pairs is equivalent to considering a κ\kappa-edge-coloring of the complete graph KnK_{n} and assigning an ordering to the colors. For odd nn, κ=n\kappa=n suffices, and for even nn, κ=n−1\kappa=n-1 suffices [40]. (Using the geometrical construction based on regular polygons, we can define the canonical partition by placing the vertices at the vertices of the polygon in order, with the last one in the center for even nn; the parts of the partition are then ordered by their lowest element under the lexicographical ordering of the pairs of cities {u,v}\{u,v\}.) Let 𝒫col=(P1,…,Pc,…,Pκ)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{col}}=(P_{1},\ldots,P_{c},\ldots,P_{\kappa}) be the resulting ordered partition, which we call a “color partition” of the pairs of cities. For example, for n=4n=4, the partition is 𝒫col=({{1,2},{3,4}},{{1,3},{2,4}},{{1,4},{2,3}}){\mathcal{P}}_{\mathrm{col}}=\left(\left\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\right\},\left\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\right\},\left\{\{1,4\},\{2,3\}\right\}\right). For different tour positions ii, two partial unitaries UPS,i,{u,v}U_{\mathrm{PS},{i,\{u,v\}}} and UPS,i′,{u′,v′}U_{\mathrm{PS},{i^{\prime},\{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}\}}} commute if ii and i′i^{\prime} are not consecutive (|i−i′modn|>1|i-i^{\prime}\mod n|>1). Thus, for partitioning the positions, we may use the parity partition 𝒫par\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{par}}, as defined in Section 4.1. We can thus define the “color-parity” ordered partition 𝒫CP=𝒫col×𝒫par\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CP}}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{col}}\times\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{par}}, with the induced lexicographical ordering of the parts. The part Pc,oddP_{c,\mathrm{odd}} contains all UPS,i,{u,v}U_{\mathrm{PS},{i,\{u,v\}}} such that ii is odd and edge {u,v}\{u,v\} is colored cc, i.e., in PcP_{c}, and defines the unitary:

Uc,odd​(β)=∏(i,{u,v})∈Pc,oddUPS,i,{u,v}​(β),U_{c,\mathrm{odd}}(\beta)=\prod_{(i,\{u,v\})\in P_{c,\mathrm{odd}}}U_{\mathrm{PS},{i,\{u,v\}}}(\beta), (51)

where the ordering of the products does not matter because each term commutes. It is a similar case for Pc,evenP_{c,\mathrm{even}} and Uc,evenU_{c,\mathrm{even}}, and Pc,lastP_{c,\mathrm{last}} and Uc,lastU_{c,\mathrm{last}}. Thus, we have the full color-parity mixer:

UCP​(β)=U𝒫CP​-​PS​(β)=∏Pc,π∈𝒫CPUc,π,U_{\mathrm{CP}}(\beta)=U_{\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CP}}\text{-}\mathrm{PS}}(\beta)=\prod_{P_{c,\pi}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CP}}}U_{c,\pi}, (52)

where the unitaries {Uc,π}\{U_{c,\pi}\} are applied in the order they appear in 𝒫CP\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CP}}. The color-parity partition is optimal with respect to the number of parts in the partition (exactly so for even nn and up to an additive factor of 2 for odd nn). By construction, application of this mixer to any feasible state results in a feasible state, thus satisfying the first design criterion. With regard to the second criterion, while a single application of this mixer will have nonzero transitions only between orderings that swap cities in tour positions no more than two apart, repeating the mixer sufficiently many times results in nonzero transitions between any two states representing orderings. More precisely, since any ordering can be obtained from any other with no more than n⁡(n−1)2\frac{n(n-1)}{2} adjacent swaps, alternating between odd and even swaps, n⁡(n−1)2\frac{n(n-1)}{2} repeats suffice for any 0<β<π/20<\beta<\pi/2.

5.1.2 Compilation

Encoding orderings.  We encoded orderings in two stages: First into strings, and then into bits making use of the encodings from Section 4. Here, we focus on a “direct encoding” as opposed to the “absolute encoding” that is introduced in Section 5.3. Other encodings of orderings are possible, such as the Lehmer code and inversion tables. In direct encoding, an ordering 𝜾=(ι1,…,ιn)\boldsymbol{\iota}=\left(\iota_{1},\ldots,\iota_{n}\right) is encoded directly as a string [n]n{[n]}^{n} of integers. Once in the form of strings, any of the string encodings introduced in Section 4 can be applied. We applied the one-hot encoding with n2n^{2} binary variables; the binary variable xj,ux_{j,u} indicates whether or not ιj=u\iota_{j}=u in the ordering, in other words, whether city uu is visited at the jj-th stop of the tour.

Phase separator.  We used the phase function g⁡(𝜾)=4​f​(𝜾)−(n−2)​∑u=1n∑v=1nd⁡(u,v)g(\boldsymbol{\iota})=4f(\boldsymbol{\iota})-(n-2)\sum_{u=1}^{n}\sum_{v=1}^{n}d(u,v), which translates to a phase separator encoded as:

HP(enc)=∑i=1n∑u=1n∑v=1nd⁡(u,v)​Zu,i​Zv,i+1.H_{\mathrm{P}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{u=1}^{n}\sum_{v=1}^{n}d(u,v)Z_{u,i}Z_{v,i+1}.\; (53)

The phase separating unitary corresponding to Equation (53) imparts a phase determined by the sum of the distances between successive cities to a state corresponding to a tour. This unitary can be implemented using n2​(n−1)n^{2}(n-1) two-qubit gates, which mutually commute. Using the same color-parity partition of the terms as for the color-parity ordering swap mixer, this can be done in depth 2​κ≤2​n2\kappa\leq 2n.

Mixer.  The individual value-selective ordering swap partial mixer, which swaps cities uu, vv between tour positions ii and jj, is expressed in the one-hot encoding as:

UPS,{i,j},{u,v}(enc)​(β)\displaystyle U_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}(\beta) =e−i​β​HPS,{i,j},{u,v},\displaystyle=e^{-i\beta H_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}}\;, (54)
HPS,{i,j},{u,v}(enc)\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}^{(\mathrm{enc})} =Su,i+​Sv,j+​Su,j−​Sv,i−+Su,i−​Sv,j−​Su,j+​Sv,i+,\displaystyle=S^{+}_{u,i}S^{+}_{v,j}S^{-}_{u,j}S^{-}_{v,i}+S^{-}_{u,i}S^{-}_{v,j}S^{+}_{u,j}S^{+}_{v,i}, (55)

where:

S+\displaystyle S^{+} =X+i​Y=|1⟩​⟨0|,\displaystyle=X+iY=\ket{1}\bra{0}, (56)
S−\displaystyle S^{-} =X−i​Y=|0⟩​⟨1|.\displaystyle=X-iY=\ket{0}\bra{1}. (57)

The iith adjacent value-selective swap partial mixer (Equation (47)) is the special case:

HPS,i,{u,v}(enc)\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{PS},{i,\{u,v\}}}^{(\mathrm{enc})} =Su,i+​Sv,i+1+​Su,i+1−​Sv,i−+Su,i−​Sv,i+1−​Su,i+1+​Sv,i+.\displaystyle=S^{+}_{u,i}S^{+}_{v,i+1}S^{-}_{u,i+1}S^{-}_{v,i}+S^{-}_{u,i}S^{-}_{v,i+1}S^{+}_{u,i+1}S^{+}_{v,i}\;. (58)

Each of the two terms of the form S+​S+​S−​S−S^{+}S^{+}S^{-}S^{-} in Equation (58), can be written as a sum of eight terms, each a product of 44 Pauli operators (e.g., X​X​Y​YXXYY). The color-parity partitioned ordering swap mixer of Equation (52) can be implemented using (n−1)​(n2)(n-1)\binom{n}{2} of these 4-qubit gates, implementable in depth 2​κ≤2​n2\kappa\leq 2n in these gates. The two-qubit gate circuit depth is at most 2​κ2\kappa times the depth of a compilation for such 44-qubit gates.

Initial state.  The initial state, an arbitrary ordering, can be prepared from the zero state |00​…​0⟩\ket{00\dots 0} using at most nn single-qubit XX gates.

5.2 Example: Single Machine Scheduling (SMS), Minimizing Total Squared Tardiness

Problem.  (1​|dj|​∑wj​Tj2).(1|d_{j}|\sum w_{j}T_{j}^{2}). Given a set of nn jobs with processing times 𝐩\mathbf{p}, deadlines 𝐝\mathbf{d}, and weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}, find a schedule minimizing the total weighted squared tardiness ∑j=1nwj​Tj2\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}T_{j}^{2}. The tardiness of job jj with completion time CjC_{j} is defined as Tj=max⁡{0,Cj−dj}T_{j}=\max\{0,C_{j}-d_{j}\}. Here, we took all quantities to be integers.

The configuration space and domain are the set of all orderings of the jobs. Given an ordering 𝜾\boldsymbol{\iota} of the jobs in which job ii is the σi\sigma_{i}-th job to start, the corresponding schedule 𝐬⁡(𝜾)\mathbf{s}(\boldsymbol{\iota}) is that in which each job starts as soon as the earlier jobs finish: sj​(𝜾)=∑i=1σj−1pιis_{j}(\boldsymbol{\iota})=\sum_{i=1}^{\sigma_{j}-1}p_{\iota_{i}}.

For a job ii starting at time sis_{i}, consider the expression:

minyi∈[0,di−pi]⁡(si+pi−di+yi)2={(si+pi−di)2,si+pi>di,0,otherwise.\min_{y_{i}\in[0,d_{i}-p_{i}]}{\left(s_{i}+p_{i}-d_{i}+y_{i}\right)}^{2}=\begin{cases}{\left(s_{i}+p_{i}-d_{i}\right)}^{2},&s_{i}+p_{i}>d_{i},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (59)

When the “slack” variable yi∈[0,di−pi]y_{i}\in[0,d_{i}-p_{i}] is minimized, this expression is equal to the square of the tardiness of job ii. Therefore, we recast SMS as the minimization of:

f⁡(𝜾,𝐲)=∑i=1nwi​(si​(𝜾)+pi−di+yi)2f(\boldsymbol{\iota},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}{\left(s_{i}(\boldsymbol{\iota})+p_{i}-d_{i}+y_{i}\right)}^{2} (60)

over the configuration space of orderings 𝜾\boldsymbol{\iota} and slack variables 𝒚\boldsymbol{y}.

Using the direct one-hot encoding defined in Section 5.1.2, in which xj,αx_{j,\alpha} indicates that job jj is the α\alpha-th to start, this is equivalent to :

f⁡(𝐱,𝐲)=∑i=1nwi​(si​(𝐱)+pi−di+yi)2,f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}{\left(s_{i}(\mathbf{x})+p_{i}-d_{i}+y_{i}\right)}^{2}, (61)

where:

si​(𝐱)=∑α=2nxi,α​∑j≠ipj​∑β=1α−1xj,β.s_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\alpha=2}^{n}x_{i,\alpha}\sum_{j\neq i}p_{j}\sum_{\beta=1}^{\alpha-1}x_{j,\beta}. (62)

Note Equation (61) may seem to be quartic; however, the encoding constraints ∑ixi,α=∑αxi,α=1\sum_{i}x_{i,\alpha}=\sum_{\alpha}x_{i,\alpha}=1 that come with the direct one-hot encoding imply that the quartic terms disappear in the full expansion. The objective function is thus a cubic pseudo-Boolean function, which corresponds to a 3-local diagonal Hamiltonian for the phase separator.

Mixer and initial state.  We used the same initial state preparation, and the same mixer as in TSP for mixing the ordering, in addition to any of the single-qudit mixers from Section 4.1.1 for each of the slack variables. Because the ordering and slack mixers act on separate sets of qubits (𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐲\mathbf{y}), they can be implemented in parallel. Note that the only requirement for the upper bound of the range of the slack variable yiy_{i} is that it be at least di−pi+1d_{i}-p_{i}+1. In particular, it could be 2⌈log2⁡(di−pi+1)⌉2^{\lceil\log_{2}(d_{i}-p_{i}+1)\rceil}, allowing us to use the binary encoding without modification.

5.3 SMS, Minimizing Total Tardiness

Problem.  (1​|dj|​∑wj​Tj)(1|d_{j}|\sum w_{j}T_{j}). Given a set of jobs with integer processing times 𝐩\mathbf{p}, deadlines 𝐝\mathbf{d}, and weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}, find a schedule minimizing the total weighted tardiness ∑j=1nwj​Tj\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}T_{j}.

5.3.1 Encoding and Mixer

The configuration space is the set of orderings of the jobs; the domain is the same.

Absolute and positional encodings.  In the “absolute” encoding of the ordering 𝜾=(ι1,…,ιn)\boldsymbol{\iota}=(\iota_{1},\ldots,\iota_{n}), we assigned each item ii a value si∈[0,h]s_{i}\in[0,h], where the “horizon” hh is a parameter of the encodings, such that for all i<ji<j, sιi<sιjs_{\iota_{i}}<s_{\iota_{j}}. In certain cases, there will be an item-specific horizon hih_{i} such that si∈[0,hi]s_{i}\in[0,h_{i}]. Note that in general, the relationship between encoded states and the orderings they encode is not injective, but it will be in the domains to which we apply it. Once the ordering 𝜾\boldsymbol{\iota} is encoded as a string 𝐬(𝜾)∈×i=1n[0,hi]\mathbf{s}(\boldsymbol{\iota})\in\times_{i=1}^{n}[0,h_{i}], the resulting string can be encoded using any of the string encodings previously introduced. We call the special case of the “absolute” encoding with h=nh=n the “positional” encoding; using the one-hot encoding of the resulting strings, the “direct” and “positional” encodings are the same.

Time-swap mixer.  We now introduce a mixer that is specific to the absolute encoding in which there is a single horizon hh and each job ii has a processing time pip_{i}. Let the horizon be h=∑i=1npih=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}. Each job can start between time 00 and hi=h−pih_{i}=h-p_{i}. (Other optimizations may be made on an instance-specific basis, though we neglect elaborating on these for ease of exposition.) We used a “time-swap” partial mixer that acts on absolutely encoded orderings:

HTS,t,{i,j}=|t+pj,t⟩​⟨t,t+pi|i,j+|t,t+pi⟩​⟨t+pj,t|i,j,H_{\mathrm{TS},{t,\{i,j\}}}=\Ket{t+p_{j},t}\Bra{t,t+p_{i}}_{i,j}+\Ket{t,t+p_{i}}\Bra{t+p_{j},t}_{i,j}, (63)

which swaps jobs ii and jj when they are scheduled immediately after one another, with the earlier one starting at time tt. To swap them regardless of the time at which the earlier one starts, we used:

HTS,{i,j}=∑t=0h−pi−pjHTS,t,{i,j}.H_{\mathrm{TS},\{i,j\}}=\sum_{t=0}^{h-p_{i}-p_{j}}H_{\mathrm{TS},{t,\{i,j\}}}. (64)

The simultaneous time-swap mixer is constructed as usual:

U𝒫​-​TS​(β)=e−i​β​HTS,U_{\mathcal{P}\text{-}\mathrm{TS}}(\beta)=e^{-i\beta H_{\mathrm{TS}}}, (65)

where HTS=∑{i,j}∈([n]2)HTS,{i,j}H_{\mathrm{TS}}=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in\binom{[n]}{2}}H_{\mathrm{TS},{\{i,j\}}}. Note that while the simultaneous versions of the total time-swap and adjacent permutation mixers are exactly the same, and in particular:

HTS,{i,i′}=∑j=1n−1HPS,j,{i,i′},H_{\mathrm{TS},{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}}=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}H_{\mathrm{PS},{j,\{i,i^{\prime}\}}}, (66)

the individual partial mixer HTS,t,{i,j}H_{\mathrm{TS},{t,\{i,j\}}} has no equivalent that acts on the unencoded ordering, because it acts depending on the total processing times of the preceding jobs rather than their number.

Now consider the “time–color” ordered partition 𝒫TC=[0,h]×[κ]\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{TC}}=[0,h]\times[\kappa], where, as in Section 5.1.1, we used a particular κ\kappa-edge-coloring of the complete graph. (Again, further optimizations may be made on an instance-specific basis.) The partition Pt,cP_{t,c} contains the partial time-swap mixers UTS,t,{i,j}U_{\mathrm{TS},{t,\{i,j\}}} for which the edge {i,j}\{i,j\} is colored cc. The full “time–color” mixer is:

UTS​(β)=∏t=0h∏c=1κU(t,c)​-​TS​(β),U_{\mathrm{TS}}(\beta)=\prod_{t=0}^{h}\prod_{c=1}^{\kappa}U_{(t,c)\text{-}\mathrm{TS}}(\beta), (67)

where U(t,c)​-​TSU_{(t,c)\text{-}\mathrm{TS}} is the product of the (mutually commuting) partial mixers in the part Pt,cP_{t,c}.

5.3.2 Mapping and Compilation

We used absolute one-hot encoding, in which the ordering is encoded as a string using absolute encoding and then the string is further encoded using one-hot encoding. Specifically, we encoded an ordering 𝜾\boldsymbol{\iota} into ∏i(hi−1)≤n​h\prod_{i}(h_{i}-1)\leq nh qubits, where qubit (i,t)(i,t) indicates if job ii starts at time tt:

|𝜾⟩↦⨂i=1n[|0⟩⊗(si−1)​|1⟩​|0⟩⊗(hi−si)].\ket{\boldsymbol{\iota}}\mapsto\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\left[{\ket{0}}^{\otimes(s_{i}-1)}\ket{1}{\ket{0}}^{\otimes(h_{i}-s_{i})}\right]. (68)

Phase separator.  The objective function is the weighted total tardiness:

f⁡(𝜾)=∑i=1nwi​max⁡{0,di−si​(𝜾)−pi}.f(\boldsymbol{\iota})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\max\{0,d_{i}-s_{i}(\boldsymbol{\iota})-p_{i}\}. (69)

This yields the encoded phase Hamiltonian:

HP(enc)=∑i=1nwi​∑t=di−pi+1hi(t+pi−di)​Zi,t.H_{\mathrm{P}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\sum_{t=d_{i}-p_{i}+1}^{h_{i}}(t+p_{i}-d_{i})Z_{i,t}. (70)

Mixer.  The partial time-swap mixer:

HTS,t,{i,j}=|t+pj,t⟩​⟨t,t+pi|i,j+|t,t+pi⟩​⟨t+pj,t|i,jH_{\mathrm{TS},{t,\{i,j\}}}=\Ket{t+p_{j},t}\Bra{t,t+p_{i}}_{i,j}+\Ket{t,t+p_{i}}\Bra{t+p_{j},t}_{i,j} (71)

in absolute one-hot encoding is equivalent to:

HTS,t,{i,j}(enc)=Si,t+pj+​Sj,t+​Si,t−​Sj,t+pi−+Si,t+​Sj,t+pi+​Si,t+pj−​Sj,t−.H_{\mathrm{TS},{t,\{i,j\}}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=S^{+}_{i,t+p_{j}}S^{+}_{j,t}S^{-}_{i,t}S^{-}_{j,t+p_{i}}+S^{+}_{i,t}S^{+}_{j,t+p_{i}}S^{-}_{i,t+p_{j}}S^{-}_{j,t}. (72)

Using the time–color partitioned time-swap mixer, this corresponds to a circuit of h​(n2)h\binom{n}{2} 4-qubit gates in depth h​κh\kappa.

Initial state.  We used an arbitrary ordering of the jobs as the initial state.

5.4 SMS, with Release Dates

Problem.  (1|dj,rj|∗)(1|d_{j},r_{j}|*). Given a set of jobs with integer processing times 𝐩\mathbf{p}, deadlines 𝐝\mathbf{d}, release times 𝐫\mathbf{r}, and weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}, find a schedule that minimizes some function of the tardiness, such that each job starts no earlier than its release time.

We considered SMS problems with release times rjr_{j}. We do not specify the objective function here, as any of those used in previous sections are still applicable. Our focus in this section is to introduce a modification of the time-swap mixer that preserves feasibility with release times.

Let the horizon hh be some upper bound on the maximum completion time, e.g., maxj⁡dj+∑jpj\max_{j}d_{j}+\sum_{j}p_{j}. Let bj=h+∑i=1j−1pib_{j}=h+\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}p_{i} be a special “buffer” time for job jj. Let Wj=[rj,h−pj]W_{j}=[r_{j},h-p_{j}] be the window of times in which job jj can start.

Consider the configuration space ×j=1n[Wj∪{bj}]\times_{j=1}^{n}\left[W_{j}\cup\{b_{j}\}\right], i.e., schedules {𝐬}\{\mathbf{s}\} in which a job is scheduled either between its release time and the horizon or at its buffer time slot. The domain is the subset of the configuration space that satisfies the problem constraint that no two jobs overlap.

5.4.1 Partial Mixer: Controlled Null-Swap Mixer

We now introduce a mixer, specifically a controlled null-swap mixer as used for graph coloring in Section 4.3, that preserves feasibility and avoids getting “stuck”:

HNS,i,t=(|bi⟩​⟨t|i+|t⟩​|bi⟩)​∏j≠i(Ij−∑t′∈nbhdi,t​(j)|t′⟩​⟨t′|j),H_{\mathrm{NS},{i,t}}=\left(\Ket{b_{i}}\Bra{t}_{i}+\Ket{t}\Ket{b_{i}}\right)\prod_{j\neq i}\left(I_{j}-\sum_{t^{\prime}\in\mathrm{nbhd}_{i,t}(j)}\Ket{t^{\prime}}\Bra{t^{\prime}}_{j}\right), (73)

which corresponds to the unitary:

UNS,i,t​(β)=Λ𝐬¯nbhdi,t​(j)​(e−i​β​(|bi⟩​⟨t|i+|t⟩​⟨bi|)+∑t′∈Wi∖{t}|t′⟩​⟨t′|)U_{\mathrm{NS},{i,t}}(\beta)=\Lambda_{\bar{\mathbf{s}}_{\mathrm{nbhd}_{i,t}(j)}}\left(e^{-i\beta\left(\Ket{b_{i}}\Bra{t}_{i}+\Ket{t}\Bra{b_{i}}\right)}+\sum_{t^{\prime}\in W_{i}\setminus\{t\}}\Ket{t^{\prime}}\Bra{t^{\prime}}\right) (74)

where:

nbhdi,t​(j)=[max⁡{t−pj+1,rj},t+pi−1]\mathrm{nbhd}_{i,t}(j)=\left[\max\{t-p_{j}+1,r_{j}\},t+p_{i}-1\right] (75)

is the temporal “neighborhood” of job ii at time tt with respect to job jj, i.e., the set of times at which starting job jj would conflict with job ii, and 𝐬nbhdi,t=((sj,t′)t′∈nbhdi,t​(j))j≠i\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{nbhd}_{i,t}}={\left({\left(s_{j,t^{\prime}}\right)}_{t^{\prime}\in\mathrm{nbhd}_{i,t}(j)}\right)}_{j\neq i}. The role of the buffer site is similar to the “uncolored” option in finding the maximal colorable induced subgraph in Section 4.3. Such mixing terms enables jobs to move freely in and out [0,T0][0,T_{0}] without inducing job overlap, hence enabling exploration of the whole feasible subspace. Recall the controlled unitary notation Λ𝐲​(Q)\Lambda_{\bf y}(Q) is defined in Equation (18) in Section 4.2.

5.4.2 Encoding and Compilation

Given the ∑i=1n|Wi|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|W_{i}\right| partial mixers, one for each job ii and time t∈Wit\in W_{i}, we can define simultaneous and sequential mixers as above. Using one-hot encoding, the partial mixer Hamiltonian is:

HNS,i,t(enc)=(∏j≠i∏t′∈nbhdi,t​(j)I+Zj,t′2)​(Xi,t​Xi,bi+Yi,t​Yi,bi).H_{\mathrm{NS},{i,t}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=\left(\prod_{j\neq i}\prod_{t^{\prime}\in\mathrm{nbhd}_{i,t}(j)}\frac{I+Z_{j,t^{\prime}}}{2}\right)\left(X_{i,t}X_{i,b_{i}}+Y_{i,t}Y_{i,b_{i}}\right)\;. (76)

The controlled null-swap can be further compiled using ancilla qubits, as in Section 4.2. While the cost of compilation could be bounded based on the degree of the graph, the overlap of the various partial mixers may be more complicated (with respect to partitioning into disjoint sets) and expensive (with respect to number of gates and ancilla qubits) depending on the SMS instance.

Objective function.  As an example objective function, we again considered minimizing the weighted total tardiness, Equation (69). The one-hot encoded phase Hamiltonian takes the form of Equation (70), with bjb_{j} included in the summation range of tt:

HP(enc)=∑i=1nwi[(bi−di)Zi,bi+∑t=di−pi+1hi(t+pi−di)Zi,t,]H_{\mathrm{P}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\left[(b_{i}-d_{i})Z_{i,b_{i}}+\sum_{t=d_{i}-p_{i}+1}^{h_{i}}(t+p_{i}-d_{i})Z_{i,t},\right] (77)

and the corresponding unitary can be implemented with ∑j(hj−dj+1)\sum_{j}(h_{j}-d_{j}+1) single qubit ZZ-rotation gates.

Initial state.  Any feasible schedule can be used as the initial state. In particular, we used a greedy earliest-release-date schedule. Assume without loss of generality that the jobs are ordered by their release times, i.e., r1≤r2≤⋯≤rnr_{1}\leq r_{2}\leq\cdots\leq r_{n}. Then set s1=r1s_{1}=r_{1} and recursively set si=max⁡{ri,si−1+pi−1}s_{i}=\max\{r_{i},s_{i-1}+p_{i-1}\}, which is feasible though likely suboptimal.

5.4.3 Mapping Variants

In the construction above, each job jj is assigned a “buffer” time bjb_{j}, and a phase bj−djb_{j}-d_{j} applied whenever that job is scheduled at its buffer time. The factor bj−djb_{j}-d_{j} is arbitrary. Rather than considering schedules in which some jobs are at their buffer time, one could consider “partial schedules”, in which a job is either scheduled at a time between 00 and hh or is in its buffer. The phase applied when a job is in its buffer need not be bj−djb_{j}-d_{j} but in fact can be arbitrary, e.g., some common “buffer phase factor” BB. In this case, we must define a scheme for associating each partial schedule with a canonical complete schedule, e.g., greedily starting the buffered jobs after those that are already scheduled. In this way, the states corresponding to partial schedules can still be considered as part of the domain.

6 Conclusions

We introduced a quantum alternating operator ansatz (QAOA), an extension of Farhi et al.’s quantum approximate optimization algorithm, and showed how to apply the ansatz to a diverse set of optimization problems with hard constraints. The essence of this extension is the consideration of general parameterized families of unitaries rather than only those corresponding to the time evolution of a local Hamiltonian, which allows it to represent a larger, and potentially more useful, set of states than the original formulation. In particular, refocusing on unitaries rather than Hamiltonians in the specification allows for more efficiently implementable mixing operators.

The original algorithm is already a leading candidate quantum heuristic for exploration on near-term hardware; our extension makes early testing on emerging gate-model quantum processors possible for a wider array of problems at an earlier stage. After formally introducing the ansatz, and providing design criteria for its components, we worked through a number of examples in detail, illustrating design techniques and exhibiting a variety of mixing operators. In the appendix, we provide a compendium of QAOA mappings for over 2020 problems, organized by type of mixer.

While the approach of designing mixing operators to keep the evolution within the feasible subspace appears quite general, as illustrated by the wide variety of examples we have worked out, it is not universally applicable. Many of the problems in Zuckerman [41] have the form of optimizing a quantity within a feasible subspace consisting of the solutions to an NP-complete problem. Not only is an initial starting state (corresponding to one or more feasible solutions) hard to find, designing the mixing operator is also problematic. Even given a set of feasible solutions to an NP-complete problem, it is typically computationally difficult to find another [42], making it difficult to design a mixer that fully explores the feasible subspace. The situation here is somewhat subtle, with it being easy to show in the case of SAT that finding a second solution when given a first remains NP-complete, but for a Hamiltonian cycle on cubic graphs, given a first solution, a second is easy to find (but not a third). See References [43, 44] for results on the complexity of “another solution problems” (ASPs). This difficulty in mapping Zuckerman’s problems to QAOA further illustrates reasons for the difficulty of these approximate optimization problems.

While we have given basic design criteria for initial states, mixing operators, and phase-separation operators, we have barely scratched the surface in terms of which possibilities perform better than others. For most of the example problems, we discussed multiple mixers, coming from different partitions and orderings of partial mixers, different choices related to connectivity, or different numbers of repeats of operators. Analytic, numerical, and ultimately experimental work is required to understand which of these mixers are most effective, and also to determine potential trade-offs with respect to robustness to noise or control error, efficiency of implementation, effectiveness of the mixing, and difficulty in optimizing the parameters. Similar questions arise with respect to choosing an initial state. An important future research direction is to explore the trade-offs between different mixing operator designs, in particular how a mixer’s connectivity relates to its effectiveness in different settings. Of particular interest is whether or not allocating resources to more complicated mixing operators at the expense of overall QAOA circuit depth results in enhanced performance. Similarly, whether kk-local mixers can be sufficiently advantageous to warrant their increased gate complexity remains to be explored. How the efficiency of different mixers depends on the underlying mixing graph (e.g., ring vs. fully-connected mixers) is studied for graph coloring problems in a forthcoming paper.

Effective parameter setting remains a critical, but mostly open, area of research. While for fixed pp, brute-force search of parameter search space was proposed [1], it is practical only for small values of pp; as pp increases, the parameter optimization becomes inefficient due to the curse of dimensionality, Guerreschi et al. [33] providing a detailed analysis. In certain simple [21] or highly symmetric [19] cases, some insight into parameter setting for p>1p>1 has been obtained, but even in the simplest cases, understanding good choices of parameters seems nontrivial [21]. Improved parameter setting protocols may come from adapting techniques from existing control theory and parameter optimization methods, and through using insights gained from classical simulation of quantum circuits and experimentation on quantum hardware as it becomes available. In particular, classical simulation of the quantum circuits can take advantage of the local structure of the objective function (when it is indeed local) and the feasibility of classically simulating the measurement of log⁡(n)\log(n)-qubits in a QAOA circuit by adapting results for IQP circuits [45].

To run on near-term quantum hardware, further compilation will be required. In many cases, we have left the compilation at the level of multiqubit operators that need to be further compiled to the gate set natively available on the hardware, most likely certain one- and two-qubit gates. Clearly, issues such as connectivity will be critical to the implementability and success of QAOA circuits. Furthermore, near-term hardware will have additional restrictions, including which qubits each gate can be applied to, the duration and fidelity of the gates, and cross-talk, among others. This necessitates additional compilation, especially to optimize success probability on pre-fault-tolerant devices. Other architectures, e.g., ones based on higher-dimensional qudits, may prompt other sorts of compilations as well. Recently, approaches for compiling quantum circuits, including QAOA circuits, to realistic hardware have been explored [22, 35, 46], but that research direction remains open to innovation. An interesting research direction is to explore the power of quantum alternating operator ansatz states built from natively available gates and directly incorporating the connectivity of the underlying hardware.

The robustness of these circuits to realistic error requires further exploration. In the near term, the question is how robust QAOA circuits are to realistic noise and how best to incorporate resource-efficient techniques to improve the robustness. In the longer term, the question becomes how to best incorporate the full spectrum of error correction techniques into this framework.

We expect some cross-fertilization between research on QAOA and research on AQO and quantum annealing, especially in the p≫0p\gg 0 regime. A particularly fruitful area of further study would be to build on the results of Yang et al. [18]. They used Pontryagin’s minimization principle to show that a bang–bang schedule is (essentially) always optimal, providing support for QAOA, and gate-based approaches, generally. However, the argument does not provide an efficient means to find such a schedule. Thus, how to find effective schedules remains open in the AQO realm, with it currently being completely open as to whether allowing non-bang–bang schedules makes the finding of good schedule parameters easier. Similarly, exploiting certain structural commonalities with VQE is likely to be fruitful. In the small pp regime, we expect further cross-fertilization between QAOA and other models being considered for early quantum supremacy experiments, such as random circuits, boson sampling, and IQP circuits. Results for IQP circuits, whose close structural similarities with QAOA circuits have already provided insights [17], and whose advanced status with respect to error analysis and fault tolerance [47, 48] are likely to prove especially useful.

A number of extensions are possible. We briefly mentioned two classes. The first is hybrid methods. As one example, some other algorithm, either classical or quantum, could be run first in order to provide a good initial state, and QAOA then used to improve upon it; this could be repeated several times with different initial states when the other algorithm is stochastic. Another example of a hybrid method is a parameter-setting protocol, in which a classical algorithm uses the results of measurements during and after runs of a QAOA circuit to iteratively improve the parameters. A second class of extensions is versions of QAOA with many parameters. For example, we introduced mixing operators that are repeated applications of some basic mixer; each application could use a different parameter. The same could be done with mixers consisting of many partial mixers. Until we have a better grasp of parameter setting in the single parameter per mixing operator case, and for the effectiveness of the different mixers, it makes sense to restrict to the simple case. The one exception is to take advantage of the specific gates natively available, and to use essentially a VQE approach, as suggested in Reference [26]. That approach makes excellent use of the capabilities of near-term hardware but may be more limited than single-parameter-per-phase QAOA in what it can tell us about parameter setting and the design of scalable quantum heuristics.

The biggest open question is the effectiveness of this approach as a quantum heuristic, and its potential impact in broadening the array of established applications of quantum computing. In particular, whether or not this approach—or quantum algorithms generally—can provide advantages for approximate optimization in terms of either approximability or computational efficiency remains a fundamental yet tantalizing open problem. While obtaining further analytic results may be possible in some cases, in general, we will have to try it out and see. Improved simulation techniques for quantum circuits, including potentially approaches tailored to QAOA circuits, can provide some insight, but the ultimate test will be experimentation on quantum hardware itself.

Appendix A Compendium of Mappings and Compilations

We summarize QAOA mappings for a variety of problems. All problems considered are in NPO [49, 50]. Problem names are compact versions of the names in Ausiello et al. [50] unless a different reference is given. Most of the mappings are new to this paper; for the exceptions, a reference is given, though in all such cases only H-QAOA mappings have been considered previously. Approximability results are taken from Ausiello et al. [50] unless otherwise mentioned.

We specify partial mixing Hamiltonians for each problem, which can then be used to define two types of full mixers, simultaneous mixers in H-QAOA that correspond to time evolution under the sum of the partial mixing Hamiltonians, and partitioned mixers (which in general are not in H-QAOA) that correspond to products of unitary operators defined by all the partial mixers in an order specified by an ordered partition, possibly repeated. We will not specify the full mixers, since they are straightforward to derive from the partial mixers. For each problem, we provide a compilation with resource counts for at least one mixer or a class of mixers. In most cases, we mention only one partial mixer and compilation, though as we have seen, there are many possibilities for partial mixers, and for compilations of the operators. For the phase operators, we employed affine transformations of the objective functions where possible to eliminate constants and identitied terms as described in the main text. A rigorous approach to constructing phase operators is given in Reference [5].

The resource counts given are upper bounds. We have not worked to find optimal compilations. For the simpler problems that have the potential for implementation in the near term, we give exact resource bounds when we have such results, rather than only giving the complexity. We give bounds for the number of computational qubits required, and also for the number of ancilla qubits, when used. We give resource counts for the number of arbitrary two-qubit gates required to implement a given operator, merging single qubit operations into two-qubit gates before or after when possible. We computed the depth for such circuits, which gives a lower bound on the circuit depth on near-term hardware, which will generally be higher due to connectivity and other constraints. In many cases, we did not compile all the way down to two-qubit gates, but instead specified the resource count in terms of multiqubit operators which would then yield a two-qubit gate count and depth given compilations of those multiqubit mixers. Throughout, the initial state is always obtained by applying a constant-depth circuit to the state |0⟩⊗⁣∗\Ket{0}^{\otimes*}.

An algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} achieves an approximation ratio r≤1r\leq 1 if for all instances xx of a maximization problem it satisfies 𝒜⁡(x)/OPT⁡(x)≥r\mathcal{A}(x)/\mathrm{OPT}(x)\geq r, where OPT⁡(x)\mathrm{OPT}(x) is the optimal solution of the given instance. Both cases in which rr is constant and in which rr is a function of the problem parameters were considered. For minimization problems, the approximation ratio is similarly defined with r≥1r\geq 1 and 𝒜⁡(x)/OPT⁡(x)≤r\mathcal{A}(x)/\mathrm{OPT}(x)\leq r. Unfortunately, there are multiple conventions in the literature, with the approximation ratio given as 1/r1/r for minimization, maximization, or both. Fortunately, there is no ambiguity for a given value of rr to which convention is being used. Here, instead of being internally consistent, we simply took the ratio as stated in the reference cited so as to facilitate easy comparison with the literature. All approximation results below concern efficient classical algorithms. Quantifying the performance of QAOA for these problems remains an important future research direction.

For all problems on a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), let |V|=n|V|=n, |E|=m|E|=m, and DGD_{G} be the maximum vertex degree.

A.1 Bit-Flip (XX) Mixers

In this section, we consider problems where all states of the configuration space are feasible, and hence the original QAOA construction may be used. Specifically, for all problems we can use the following:
Variables: nn binary variables.
Initial state: |0⟩⊗n\ket{0}^{\otimes n} or |+⟩⊗n\ket{+}^{\otimes n}.
Mixer: The standard mixer UMH​(β)=e−i​β​BU_{\mathrm{M}}^{H}(\beta)=e^{-i\beta B},
where B=∑j=1mXjB=\sum_{j=1}^{m}X_{j}, which can be implemented with depth 11. (Since all terms commute and act on separate qubits, we do not need to consider partitioned variants of the standard mixer.)
Phase separator: UP​(γ)=exp⁡[−i​γ​HP]U_{\mathrm{P}}(\gamma)=\exp[-i\gamma H_{\mathrm{P}}], where we specify HPH_{\mathrm{P}} for each problem.
All problems in this section can be trivially extended to their weighted version by multiplying the terms of the phase Hamiltonian by the corresponding weights.

A.1.1 Maximum Cut

Problem: Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), find a subset S⊂VS\subset V such that the number of edges between SS and V∖SV\setminus S is the largest.
Prior QAOA work: Numerical [1] and analytical [21] results obtained for p=1p=1.
Approximability: APX-complete [51, 52]. NP-hard to approximate better than 16/1716/17 [53]. Semidefinite programming achieves 0.87850.8785 [54], which is optimal under the unique games conjecture [55]. On bounded degree graphs with DG≥3D_{G}\geq 3, it can be approximated to within 0.8785+O⁡(DG)0.8785+O(D_{G}) [56], in particular to 0.9210.921 for DG=3D_{G}=3, but remains APX-complete [51].
Configuration space, Domain, and Encoding: {0,1}n{\{0,1\}}^{n}, indicating whether each vertex is in SS or not.
Objective: max|{{u,v}∈E:u∈S,v∉S}|\max\left|\left\{\{u,v\}\in E:u\in S,v\notin S\right\}\right|.
Phase separator: HP=∑{u,v}∈EZu​ZvH_{\mathrm{P}}=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}Z_{u}Z_{v}.
Resource count for phase separator: mm gates with depth at most DG+1D_{G}+1.
Variant: Directed-MaxCut (Max-Directed-Cut), where we seek to maximize the number of the directed edges leaving SS. The phase separator is replaced by HP=∑(u,v)∈E(Zu−Zv+Zu​Zv)H_{\mathrm{P}}=\sum_{(u,v)\in E}(Z_{u}-Z_{v}+Z_{u}Z_{v}).

A.1.2 Max-ℓ\ell-SAT

Problem: Given mm disjunctive clauses over nn Boolean variables 𝐱\bf x, where each clause contains at most ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 literals, find a variable assignment that maximizes the number of satisfied clauses. Let 𝐱α\mathbf{x}_{\alpha} be the variables involved in clause α\alpha and Cα​(𝐱α)=1C_{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}_{\alpha})=1 (00) if the state of 𝐱α\mathbf{x}_{\alpha} (resp., does not) satisfies the clause.
Prior QAOA work: Considered in Reference [20].
Approximability: APX-complete [51]. The best classical approximation ratio for Max-22-Sat is 0.9400.940 [57], which cannot be improved beyond 0.9430.943 under the unique games conjecture [55], or beyond 0.9540.954 unless P=N​PP=NP [53]. For Max-33-Sat, an efficient 7/87/8-approximation [58] is known, which is optimal unless P=N​PP=NP [53]. Remains APX-complete when any literal appears in at most 33 clauses [50].
Objective: max∑j=αmCα(𝐱α)\max\sum_{j=\alpha}^{m}C_{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}_{\alpha}).
Phase separator: HP=∑α=1mHCα​(𝐱α)H_{\mathrm{P}}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{m}H_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{x}_{\alpha}).
Resource count for phase separator: Can be implemented with (ℓk)\binom{\ell}{k} many kk-local ZZ⋯ZZZ\cdots Z gates, for k=1,…,ℓk=1,\ldots,\ell, overall requiring at most O⁡(m​2ℓ)O(m2^{\ell}) two-qubit gates.

A.1.3 Min-ℓ\ell-SAT

Problem: The same as Max-ℓ\ell-SAT, except with minimization instead of maximization of the number of satisfied clauses.
Approximability: APX-complete [59]. Unless P=N​PP=NP, no classical algorithm can do better than 1.36061.3606 for MinSAT [60], or, for Min-ℓ\ell-SAT, better than 15/14≃1.071415/14\simeq 1.0714 for k=2k=2 or 7/6≃1.16677/6\simeq 1.1667 for arbitrary ℓ\ell [61]. On the other hand, constructive algorithms are known which achieve approximation ratios of 1.10371.1037, 1.21361.2136, and 1−21−ℓ1-2^{1-\ell} for Min-22-SAT, Min-33-SAT, and Min-ℓ\ell-SAT, respectively [61, 62].
Mapping: The same as Max-ℓ\ell-SAT.

A.1.4 Max-Not-All-Equal-ℓ\ell-SAT (NAE-ℓ\ell-SAT)

Problem: The same as in Max-ℓ\ell-SAT, except that in NAE-ℓ\ell-SAT, each clause is satisfied only if all ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3 variables do not all have the same value.
Approximability: APX-complete [51]. A classical 1.381.38-approximation algorithm is known [63]. For ℓ=3\ell=3 approximable to 1.1381.138 but no better than 1.0901.090 [64, 50].
Mapping: Same as Max-ℓ\ell-SAT but with a slight modification of the phase operator; see, e.g., [5].
Variant: Similar considerations apply to Max-11-in-ℓ\ell-Sat, in which a clause is satisfied when exactly one of its variables is true.

A.1.5 Set Splitting

Problem: Given a set 𝒮\cal S and a collection of subsets {Sj}j=1m{\{S_{j}\}}_{j=1}^{m}, seek a partition 𝒮=𝒮1∪(𝒮∖𝒮1){\cal S}={\cal S}_{1}\cup({\cal S}\setminus{\cal S}_{1}) that maximizes the number of split sets, i.e., subsets SjS_{j} with elements in both 𝒮1{\cal S}_{1} and 𝒮∖𝒮1{\cal S}\setminus{\cal S}_{1}.
Approximability: APX-complete [65]. Can be approximated to 0.74990.7499 [66]. Remains APX-complete if each SjS_{j} is restricted to having at most or exactly k≥2k\geq 2 elements [67]. For each SjS_{j} having exactly k≥4k\geq 4 elements, unless P=N​PP=NP, there is no efficient classical algorithm that does essentially better than a random partition [53, 68]. The generalization MaxHypergraphCut, in which each subset is given a weight and we seek to maximize the total weight of the split sets, can be approximated to 0.74990.7499 [66].
Reduction to Not-All-Equal-ℓ\ell-SAT: This problem is a special case of NAE-ℓ\ell-SAT, where none of the variables are negated.

A.1.6 E3Lin2

Problem: Given a set of mm three-variable equations 𝒜={Aj}{\cal A}=\{A_{j}\}, over nn binary variables 𝐱∈{0,1}n\mathbf{x}\in{\{0,1\}}^{n}, where each equation AjA_{j} is of the form xa1,j+xa2,j+xa3,j=bjmod2x_{a_{1,j}}+x_{a_{2,j}}+x_{a_{3,j}}=b_{j}\mod 2 where a1,j,a2,j,a3,j∈[n]a_{1,j},\penalty\ a_{2,j},\penalty\ a_{3,j}\in[n] and bj∈{0,1}b_{j}\in\{0,1\}, find an assignment 𝐱∈{0,1}n\mathbf{x}\in{\{0,1\}}^{n} that maximizes the number of satisfied equations.
Prior QAOA work: Considered in Reference [16].
Approximability: No efficient 1+ϵ1+\epsilon classical approximation algorithm unless P=N​PP=NP [53]. For the case where each variable appears in at most DD equations, an efficient classical algorithm satisfies a 1/2+Ω(D−1/2)1/2+\Omega(D^{-1/2}) fraction of the equations [23]. Shown in Reference [16] that QAOA with p=1p=1 achieves the same result up to a factor logarithmic in DD for this case.
Objective: Maximize the number of satisfied equations.
Phase Separator: HP=∑j=1mHjH_{\mathrm{P}}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}H_{j} where Hj=(−1)bj​Za1,j​Za2,j​Za3,j.H_{j}={(-1)}^{b_{j}}Z_{a_{1,j}}Z_{a_{2,j}}Z_{a_{3,j}}\;.
Resource count for phase separator: Can be implemented with mm many 3-qubit gates.

A.2 Controlled-Bit-Flip (Λf​(X)\Lambda_{f}(X)) Mixers

All problems in this section are graph or subset problems with QAOA mappings that use controlled-bit-flip mixers on bit strings. (See Section 4.2.) Note that MaxSetPacking (Section A.2.4) reduces to MaxIndependentSet (Section A.2.1) on the constraint graph; MinVertexCover (Section A.2.3) is a special case of MinSetCover (Section A.2.5), in which the universe is the set of edges, and each subset in the collection corresponds to the edges adjacent to a single vertex; and MaxClique (Section A.2.2) is simply MaxIndependentSet on the complement graph.
Configuration space: The configuration space of each problem is the subsets V′V^{\prime} of some set VV (resp., S′⊂SS^{\prime}\subset S), represented by bitstrings 𝐱∈{0,1}n\mathbf{x}\in{\{0,1\}}^{n}, with xv=1x_{v}=1 indicating v∈V′v\in V^{\prime}.
Constraint graph: An instance of each problem is either specified by a graph or has a natural corresponding constraint graph whose vertices correspond to the variables and with respect to which each variable vv is graph-adjacent to nbhd⁡(v)\mathrm{nbhd}(v).
Domain: Elements of the configuration space that satisfy some CNF formula (whose clauses correspond to the edges of the problem or the constraint graph, except for MinSetCover) that specifies a required property.
Objective: Maximize or minimize the subset cardinality.
Mixing rule: Swap an element vv in or out of V′V^{\prime} if some predicate χ⁡(𝐱nbhd⁡(v))\chi(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{nbhd}(v)}) is satisfied by the partial state of its neighbors. (The predicate χ\chi will depend on the problem.)
Partial mixing Hamiltonian: HCX,v=Xv​HPvH_{\mathrm{CX},v}=X_{v}H_{P_{v}}, which can be used to define both a simultaneous controlled bit-flip mixer and a class of partitioned controlled bit-flip mixers. (See Section 4.2.)

A.2.1 MaxIndependentSet [Section 4.2]

Problem: Given G=(V,E)G=(V,E), maximize the size of a subset V′⊂VV^{\prime}\subset V of mutually non-adjacent vertices.
Prior QAOA work: [1]. See Section 4.2 for a detailed discussion of the mapping and generalization.
Approximability: Poly-APX-complete [69], and has no constant factor approximation unless P=N​PP=NP. On bounded degree graphs with maximum degree DG≥3D_{G}\geq 3 can be approximated to (DG+2)/3(D_{G}+2)/3 [69], but remains APX-complete [51].
Domain: Independent sets, {𝐱:⋀{u,v}∈Ex¯u∨x¯v}\left\{\mathbf{x}:\bigwedge_{\{u,v\}\in E}\bar{x}_{u}\lor\bar{x}_{v}\right\}.
Objective: max |V′|=∑v∈Vxv|V^{\prime}|=\sum_{v\in V}x_{v}.
Mixing rule: Swap vv in or out of V′V^{\prime} if none of its neighbors are in V′V^{\prime}.
Partial mixing Hamiltonian: HCX,v=Xv​H𝖭𝖮𝖱⁡(xnbhd⁡(v))H_{\mathrm{CX},v}=X_{v}H_{\mathsf{NOR}(x_{\mathrm{nbhd}(v)})}.
Phase separator: UP(γ)=exp(−iγ∑u∈VZu)U_{\mathrm{P}}(\gamma)=\exp(-i\gamma\sum_{u\in V}Z_{u}).
Initial state: |s⟩=|0⟩⊗n\ket{s}=\ket{0}^{\otimes n}, i.e., V′=∅V^{\prime}=\emptyset.
Resource count:

  • •

    Controlled-bit-flip mixers: nn multiqubit-controlled-X⁡(β)X(\beta) gates, each with at most DGD_{G} controls (exactly DvD_{v} controls for each vertex). Depth at most nn but will be much less for sparsely connected graphs.

  • •

    Phase separator: nn single-qubit ZZ-rotations. Depth 11.

Variants: Extends easily to weighted-MaxIndependentSet with objective function f=∑i=1nwi​xif=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}x_{i}.

A.2.2 MaxClique

Problem: Given G=(V,E)G=(V,E), maximize the size of a clique in GG (a subset V′⊂VV^{\prime}\subset V that induces a subgraph in which all pairs of vertices are adjacent).
Approximability: A O⁡(n/log2⁡n)O(n/\log^{2}n)-approximation is known [70], but cannot be efficiently approximated classically better than O⁡(n1−ϵ)O(n^{1-\epsilon}) for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 unless P=N​PP=NP [71].
Domain: Cliques, {𝐱:⋀{u,v}∈E⁡(G¯)x¯u∨x¯v}\left\{\mathbf{x}:\bigwedge_{\{u,v\}\in E(\overline{G})}\bar{x}_{u}\lor\bar{x}_{v}\right\}.
Objective: max |V′|=∑v∈Vxv|V^{\prime}|=\sum_{v\in V}x_{v}.
Reduction to MaxIndependentSet: Every clique on G=(V,E)G=(V,E) gives on independent set on the complement graph G¯=(V,E⁡(G¯))\overline{G}=(V,E(\overline{G})) where E⁡(G¯)=(V2)∖EE(\overline{G})=\binom{V}{2}\setminus E. Therefore, a mapping for MaxClique is given by the mapping for MaxIndependentSet applied to the complement graph G¯\overline{G}.
Resource count: The same resources as for MaxIndependentSet, except that the controlled bit-flip mixers are now multiqubit-controlled-X gates with at most n−DG−1n-D_{G}-1 controls (exactly n−Dv−1n-D_{v}-1 controls for each vertex vv).

A.2.3 MinVertexCover

Problem: Given G=(V,E)G=(V,E), minimize the size of a subset V′⊂VV^{\prime}\subset V that covers VV, i.e., for every (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E, u∈V′u\in V^{\prime} or v∈V′v\in V^{\prime}.
Prior QAOA work: A quantum walk generalization of QAOA is proposed for this problem in Reference [31].
Approximability: APX-complete [51]. Has a (2−Θ⁡(1/log⁡n))(2-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\log n}))-approximation [72] but cannot be approximated better than 1.36061.3606 unless P=N​PP=NP [73].
Domain: Vertex covers, {𝐱:⋀{u,v}∈E⁡(G¯)xu∨xv}\left\{\mathbf{x}:\bigwedge_{\{u,v\}\in E(\overline{G})}x_{u}\lor x_{v}\right\}.
Objective: min |V′||V^{\prime}|.
Initial state: |s⟩=|1⟩⊗n\ket{s}=\ket{1}^{\otimes n}, i.e., V′=VV^{\prime}=V.
Mixing rule: Swap vv in or out of V′V^{\prime} if all of the edges incident to vv are covered by V′∩nbhd⁡(v)V^{\prime}\cap\mathrm{nbhd}(v).
Phase Separator: UP(γ)=exp(−iγ∑u∈VZu)U_{\mathrm{P}}(\gamma)=\exp(-i\gamma\sum_{u\in V}Z_{u}).
Reduction to MaxIndependentSet: A subset V′⊂VV^{\prime}\subset V is a vertex cover if and only if V\V′V\backslash V^{\prime} is an independent set, so the problem of finding a minimum vertex cover is equivalent to that of finding a maximum independent set. While as approximation problems they are not equivalent [49], we can use the same mapping as for MaxIndependentSet with each x¯v\bar{x}_{v} replaced by xvx_{v}. The resource counts are the same as for MaxIndependentSet.
Reduction to MinSat: Maranthe et al. [74] give an approximation-preserving reduction to Min-DGD_{G}-SAT enabling us to use the QAOA constuction given above for MinSat. The resource counts are the same as for MinSat with mm variables and nn clauses.

A.2.4 MaxSetPacking

Problem: Given a universe [n][n] and mm subsets 𝒮=(Sj)j=1m\mathcal{S}={\left(S_{j}\right)}_{j=1}^{m}, Sj⊂[n]S_{j}\subset[n], find the maximum cardinality subcollection 𝒮′⊂𝒮\mathcal{S^{\prime}}\subset\mathcal{S} of pairwise disjoint subsets.
Approximability: As difficult as MaxClique [50]. Cannot be efficiently approximated within any constant factor unless P=N​PP=NP [75]. The best known algorithm gives an O⁡(n)O(\sqrt{n})-approximation [76]. APX-complete with the restriction |Sj|≤k|S_{j}|\leq k (Max-kk-Set-Packing).
Constraint graph: Vertices V=[m]V=[m] corresponding to elements of 𝒮\mathcal{S}, edges EE corresponding to pairs of intersecting subsets.
Domain: Subcollections containing mutually disjoint subsets, {𝐱:⋀{i,j}∈Ex¯i∨x¯j}\left\{\mathbf{x}:\bigwedge_{\{i,j\}\in E}\bar{x}_{i}\lor\bar{x}_{j}\right\}.
Objective: max |𝒮′|=∑j=1mxj|\mathcal{S}^{\prime}|=\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{j}
Initial state: |s⟩=|0⟩⊗m\ket{s}=\ket{0}^{\otimes m}, i.e., 𝒮′=∅\mathcal{S}^{\prime}=\emptyset.
Mixing rule: Swap SjS_{j} in or out of 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime} if SjS_{j} is disjoint from the other subsets in 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime}, i.e., 𝐱nbhd⁡(j)=𝟎\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{nbhd}(j)}=\mathbf{0}.
Partial mixing Hamiltonian: HCX,j=2−Dj​Xj​∏i∈nbhd⁡(j)(I+Zi)=Xj​H𝖭𝖮𝖱⁡(xnbhd⁡(j))H_{\mathrm{CX},j}=2^{-D_{j}}X_{j}\prod_{i\in\mathrm{nbhd}(j)}(I+Z_{i})=X_{j}H_{\mathsf{NOR}(x_{\mathrm{nbhd}(j)})}.
Phase separator: UP(γ)=exp(−iγ∑j=1mZj)U_{\mathrm{P}}(\gamma)=\exp(-i\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{m}Z_{j}).
Resource count:

  • •

    Controlled-bit-flip mixers: Each partial mixer HCX,jH_{\mathrm{CX},j} is implemented as a controlled-RXR_{X} gate with DjD_{j} control qubits. Partial mixer depth at most mm.

  • •

    Phase separator: mm single-qubit ZZ-rotations. Depth 11.

  • •

    Initial state: Depth 00.

Variants: Also called MaxHypergraphMatching. Equivalent to MaxClique under a PTAS-reduction [50].

A.2.5 MinSetCover

Problem: Given a universe [n][n] and mm subsets 𝒮=(Sj)j=1n\mathcal{S}={\left(S_{j}\right)}_{j=1}^{n}, Sj⊂[n]S_{j}\subset[n], find the minimum cardinality subcollection 𝒮′⊂𝒮\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{S} of the SjS_{j} such that their union recovers [n][n].
Approximability: There exists a 1+ln⁡n1+\ln n algorithm [77]. Cannot be efficiently approximated to (1−o⁡(1))​ln⁡n(1-o(1))\ln n unless P=N​PP=NP [78]. APX-complete with the restriction |Sj|≤k|S_{j}|\leq k (Max-kk-Set-Cover) [50].
Constraint graph: Vertices [m][m] corresponding to subcollections in 𝒮\mathcal{S}; two vertices {i,j}\{i,j\} are adjacent if and only if their corresponding sets intersect, Si∩Sj≠∅S_{i}\cap S_{j}\neq\emptyset.
Domain: Set covers, {𝐱:⋃j∈[m]:xj=1Sj=[n]}\left\{\mathbf{x}:\bigcup_{j\in[m]:x_{j}=1}S_{j}=[n]\right\}.
