Initial state: |s⟩=|1⟩⊗m\ket{s}=\ket{1}^{\otimes m}, i.e., 𝒮′=𝒮\mathcal{S}^{\prime}=\mathcal{S}.
Mixing rule: Swap set SjS_{j} in or out of 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime} if 𝒮′∖Sj\mathcal{S^{\prime}}\setminus S_{j} covers [n][n].
Partial mixing Hamiltonian:

HCX,j=(∏i=1n(I−∏ℓ∈[m]:ℓ≠j,i∈SℓI+Zl2))Xj=XjHχMSC,j,H_{\mathrm{CX},j}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(I-\prod_{\ell\in[m]:\ell\neq j,i\in S_{\ell}}\frac{I+Z_{l}}{2}\right)\right)X_{j}=X_{j}H_{\chi_{\mathrm{MSC,j}}}, (78)

where χMSC,j(𝐱nbhd⁡(j))=⋀i∈Sj⋁ℓ∈nbhd⁡(j):i∈Sℓxℓ\chi_{\mathrm{MSC,j}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{nbhd}(j)})=\bigwedge_{i\in S_{j}}\bigvee_{\ell\in\mathrm{nbhd}(j):i\in S_{\ell}}x_{\ell}.

Phase separator: UP(γ)=exp(−iγ∑j=1mZj)U_{\mathrm{P}}(\gamma)=\exp(-i\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{m}Z_{j}).
Resource count:

  • •

    Controlled-bit-flip mixers: For each HCX,jH_{\mathrm{CX},j}, use |Sj||S_{j}| ancilla qubits. Use each ancilla qubit ii to compute ⋁ℓ∈nbhd⁡(j):i∈Sℓxℓ\bigvee_{\ell\in\mathrm{nbhd}(j):i\in S_{\ell}}x_{\ell} using a controlled NOT gate with |{ℓ∈nbhd⁡(j):i∈Sℓ}|≤|nbhd⁡(j)|=Dj|\{\ell\in\mathrm{nbhd}(j):i\in S_{\ell}\}|\leq|\mathrm{nbhd}(j)|=D_{j} control qubits. Then implement HCX,jH_{\mathrm{CX},j} using a controlled X gate on qubit jj with the |Sj||S_{j}| ancilla qubits as the control. Finally, uncompute the ancilla qubits using the same |Sj||S_{j}| controlled NOT gates as in the first step. Depth at most 2​Dj+12D_{j}+1 per partial mixer.

  • •

    Phase separator: mm single-qubit ZZ-rotations. Depth 11.

  • •

    Initial state: Depth 00.

Variants: Equivalent to minimum hitting set [50] and under LL-reductions equivalent to minimum dominating set (which is a special case of minimum set cover).

A.3 X​YXY Mixers

In this section, we consider problems where the domain is strings of dd-dits, d≥3d\geq 3, with QAOA mappings that use XY mixers.

A.3.1 Max-κ\kappa-ColorableSubgraph [Section 4.1]

Problem: Given a graph GG and κ\kappa colors, maximize the size (number of edges) of a properly colored subgraph.
Approximability: A random coloring properly colors a fraction 1−1/κ1-1/\kappa of edges in expectation. Equivalent to MaxCut for κ=2\kappa=2. For κ>2\kappa>2, semidefinite programming gives a (1−1/κ+(2+o⁡(κ))​ln⁡κκ2)−(1-1/\kappa+\left(2+o(\kappa)\right)\frac{\ln\kappa}{\kappa^{2}})-approximation [79], which is optimal up to the o⁡(κ)o(\kappa) factor under the unique games conjecture [55]. APX-complete for κ≥2\kappa\geq 2 [51] and no PTAS exists unless P=N​PP=NP [65].
Configuration space and domain: The set of all colorings with at most κ\kappa colors, 𝐱∈[κ]n\mathbf{x}\in{[\kappa]}^{n}.
Objective: max ∑{u,v}∈E𝖭𝖤𝖰⁡(xu,xv)\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}\mathsf{NEQ}(x_{u},x_{v}).
Initial state: All vertices colored with color 11, |1⟩n\ket{1}^{n}.
Partial Mixing Hamiltonian: Hr​-​NV=∑a=1r(X˘a+(X˘†)a)H_{r\text{-}\mathrm{NV}}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}\left({\breve{X}}^{a}+{({\breve{X}}^{\dagger})}^{a}\right).
Encoding: One-hot.

  • •

    Phase Separator: UP​(γ)=∏{u,v}∈E∏j=1κexp⁡(−i​γ​Zv,j​Zv,j)U_{\mathrm{P}}(\gamma)=\prod_{\{u,v\}\in E}\prod_{j=1}^{\kappa}\exp\left(-i\gamma Z_{v,j}Z_{v,j}\right)

  • •

    Resource count:

    • –

      Number of qubits: n​κn\kappa.

    • –

      Parity ring mixer: n​κn\kappa two-qubit (X​YXY) gates, with depth at most 22 (κ\kappa even) or 33 (κ\kappa odd).

    • –

      Phase separator: n​κn\kappa two-qubit (Z​ZZZ) gates. Depth at most DG+1D_{G}+1.

    • –

      Initial state: nn single-qubit XX gates. Depth 11.

Alternative encoding (for κ=2l\kappa=2^{l}): Binary

  • •

    Phase separator: UP​(γ)=∏{u,v}∈EΛ𝖤𝖰​𝐱u,𝐯​(e−i​γ)U_{\mathrm{P}}(\gamma)=\prod_{\{u,v\}\in E}\Lambda_{\mathsf{EQ}{\mathbf{x}_{u},\mathbf{v}}}\left(e^{-i\gamma}\right)

  • •

    Mixer: UM​(β)=∏i=1ne−i​β​Xi,0​ADDi​(1)†​e−i​β​Xi,0​ADDi​(1).U_{\mathrm{M}}(\beta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}e^{-i\beta X_{i,0}}{\mathrm{ADD}_{i}(1)}^{\dagger}e^{-i\beta X_{i,0}}\mathrm{ADD}_{i}(1). where ADDi​(z)\mathrm{ADD}_{i}(z) adds zz to the register ii encoding an integer in binary.

  • •

    Resource count:

    • –

      Parity ring mixer: 2​n2n ADD\mathrm{ADD}s, 2​n2n single-qubit rotations; completely parallelizable.

    • –

      Phase separator: mm controlled-phase gates with 2​l2l controls; depth O⁡(DG)O(D_{G}).

    • –

      Initial state: nn single-qubit XX gates in depth 11.

Variants: Also known as Max-κ\kappa-Cut [79, 55], sometimes with weighted edges. For the weighted case, the same approximability results apply.

A.3.2 Graph Partitioning (Minimum Bisection)

Problem: Given a graph GG such that nn is even, find a subset V0⊂VV_{0}\subset V satisfying |V0|=n/2|V_{0}|=n/2 such that the number of edges between V0V_{0} and V∖V0V\setminus V_{0} is minimized.
Prior AQO work: Studied in the context of AQO for constrained optimization [6].
Approximability: An efficient O⁡(log1.5⁡n)O(\log^{1.5}n)-approximate algorithm is known [80].
Configuration space, domain, and encoding: Bit strings 𝐱\bf x of Hamming weight n/2n/2.
Objective: min∑{u​v}∈E𝖭𝖤𝖰(xu,xv)\min\sum_{\{uv\}\in E}\mathsf{NEQ}(x_{u},x_{v}).
Initial state: Any 𝐱\bf x of Hamming weight n/2n/2.
Phase separator: UP(γ)=exp(−iγ∑{u​v}∈EZuZv)U_{\mathrm{P}}(\gamma)=\exp(-i\gamma\sum_{\{uv\}\in E}Z_{u}Z_{v}).
Partial mixing Hamiltonian: Qubit ring XY mixer Hring(enc)=∑u=1n(Xu​Xu+1+Yu​Yu+1)H_{\mathrm{ring}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=\sum_{u=1}^{n}\left(X_{u}X_{u+1}+Y_{u}Y_{u+1}\right).
Resource count:

  • •

    Number of qubits: nn.

  • •

    Parity ring mixer: nn two-qubit (XX+YY) gates, with depth at most 2 (nn even) or 3 (nn odd).

  • •

    Phase separator: mm two-qubit (ZZ) gates. Depth at most DG+1D_{G}+1.

  • •

    Initial state: n/2n/2 single-qubit XX gates. Depth 11.

A.3.3 Maximum Bisection

Problem: Given a graph GG such that nn is even, and edge weights wjw_{j}, find a subset V0⊂VV_{0}\subset V satisfying |V0|=n/2|V_{0}|=n/2 such that the total weight of edges crossing between V0V_{0} and V∖V0V\setminus V_{0} is maximized.
Approximability: A random bisection gives an 0.50.5-approximation in expectation, improved to 0.650.65 [79].
Mapping: Same as graph partitioning (Section A.3.2) with weights included in the phase separator.

A.3.4 Maximum Vertex κ\kappa-Cover

Problem: Variant of vertex cover optimization problem. Given a graph GG and an integer κ≤n\kappa\leq n, find a subset V0⊂VV_{0}\subset V of size |V0|=κ|V_{0}|=\kappa such that the number of edges covered by V0V_{0} is maximized.
Approximability: It is NP-hard to decide whether or not a fraction (1−ϵ)(1-\epsilon) of the edges can be κ\kappa-covered [65].
Mapping: Same as graph partitioning (Section A.3.2) with the Hamming weight n/2n/2 replaced by κ\kappa.

A.4 Controlled-X​YXY Mixers

In this section, we consider problems with QAOA mappings that use controlled-XY mixers.

A.4.1 Max-κ\kappa-ColorableInducedSubgraph [Section 4.3]

Problem: Given a graph GG and κ\kappa colors, maximize the size of a subset of vertices V′⊂VV^{\prime}\subset V whose induced subgraph is κ\kappa-colorable.
Approximability: Equivalent to MaxIndependentSet for k=1k=1. Both as easy and as hard to approximate as MaxIndependentSet for k≥1k\geq 1 [81, 50]. On bounded degree graphs, can be approximated to (DG/k+1)/2(D_{G}/k+1)/2, but remains APX-complete [82].
Configuration space: [κ+1]n{[\kappa+1]}^{n}. (00-th color is “uncolored” and represents v∉V′v\notin V^{\prime}.)
Domain: κ\kappa-colorable induced subgraphs, {𝐱:⋀{i,j}∈E(𝖤𝖰⁡(xi,0)∨𝖤𝖰⁡(xj,0)∨𝖭𝖤𝖰⁡(xi,xj))}\left\{\mathbf{x}:\bigwedge_{\{i,j\}\in E}\left(\mathsf{EQ}(x_{i},0)\lor\mathsf{EQ}(x_{j},0)\lor\mathsf{NEQ}(x_{i},x_{j})\right)\right\}.
Objective: min ∑i=1n𝖭𝖤𝖰⁡(xi,0)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{NEQ}(x_{i},0).
Initial state: All vertices uncolored, |10​…​0⟩⊗n\ket{10\dots 0}^{\otimes n}.
Mixing rule: A vertex can switch between being uncolored and colored jj only if none of its neighbours are colored jj.
Partial mixing Hamiltonian: Controlled null-swap mixer at a vertex.
Encoding: One-hot.
Phase separator: UP​(γ)=exp⁡(i2​γ​∑u∈V∑j=1κZu,j)U_{\mathrm{P}}(\gamma)=\exp(\frac{i}{2}\gamma\sum_{u\in V}\sum_{j=1}^{\kappa}Z_{u,j}).
Resource count:

  • •

    Partitioned controlled null-swap mixers: n​κn\kappa partial mixers, each acting on at most DG+1D_{G}+1 qubits. Depth at most n​κn\kappa but will be much less for sparsely connected graphs.

  • •

    Phase separator: nn single-qubit ZZ-rotations. Depth 11.

  • •

    Initial state: |s⟩=(|1⟩⊗|0⟩⊗κ)⊗n\ket{s}={\left(\ket{1}\otimes{\ket{0}}^{\otimes\kappa}\right)}^{\otimes n}, implemented in depth 11 with nn XX gates.

A.4.2 MinGraphColoring [Section 4.4]

Problem: Given a graph GG, minimize the number of colors required to properly color it.
Approximability: The best classical algorithm [83] achieves approximation ratio O⁡(n​(log⁡log⁡n)2log3⁡n)O(n\frac{{(\log\log n)}^{2}}{\log^{3}n}), and we cannot do better than n1−ϵn^{1-\epsilon} for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 unless P=N​PP=NP [71]. For edge-colorings of multigraphs, there is a (1.1+0.8/κ∗1.1+0.8/\kappa^{*})-approximate algorithm [84].
Configuration space: [κ]n{[\kappa]}^{n}, κ=DG+2\;\kappa=D_{G}+2.
Domain: Proper κ\kappa-colorings of GG (many of which use fewer than κ\kappa colors), {𝐱:⋀{i,j}∈E𝖭𝖤𝖰⁡(xi,xj)}\left\{\mathbf{x}:\bigwedge_{\{i,j\}\in E}\mathsf{NEQ}(x_{i},x_{j})\right\}.
Objective: Minimize number of used colors: ∑a=1κ𝖮𝖱⁡(𝖤𝖰⁡(x1,a),…,𝖤𝖰⁡(xn,a))\sum_{a=1}^{\kappa}\mathsf{OR}(\mathsf{EQ}(x_{1},a),\ldots,\mathsf{EQ}(x_{n},a)).
Mixing rule: The color of vertex uu may be swapped between colors cc and c′c^{\prime} if none of its neighbours are already colored cc or c′c^{\prime}.
Partial mixing Hamiltonian: Controlled-swap partial mixing Hamiltonian.
Encoding: One-hot.
Phase separator: ∏a=1κΛ𝖮𝖱⁡(𝐱[n],a)​(e−i​γ)\prod_{a=1}^{\kappa}\Lambda_{\mathsf{OR}(\mathbf{x}_{[n],a})}\left(e^{-i\gamma}\right).
Resource count:

  • •

    Partitioned controlled-swap mixers: κ⁡(κ−1)​n/2\kappa(\kappa-1)n/2 controlled gates on no more than DG+2D_{G}+2 qubits.

  • •

    Phase separator: κ\kappa partial phase separators acting on n+1n+1 qubits, one target qubit and nn control qubits. Depth 22 in partial phase separators, or depth 11 with the addition of κ\kappa ancilla qubits.

  • •

    Initial state: Any valid κ\kappa coloring (can be efficiently computed classically). Can be implemented in depth 11 using nn single-qubit XX gates.

Reduction from MinEdgeColoring: In MinEdgeColoring, the objective is to minimize the number of colors needed to color the edges so that no two adjacent edges have the same color. This is equivalent to MinGraphColoring on the line graph.

A.4.3 MinCliqueCover

Problem: Given a graph GG, we seek the smallest collection of cliques S1,…,Sk⊂VS_{1},\ldots,S_{k}\subset V, such that every vertex belongs to at least one clique.
Approximability: If MaxClique is approximable within f⁡(n)f(n) for a given instance, then MinCliqueCover approximable to O⁡(f⁡(n))O(f(n)) [50]. Not approximable within nϵn^{\epsilon} for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 [85].
Reduction to MinGraphColoring: A partition of the vertices of GG is a kk-clique cover if and only if it is a proper kk-coloring of the complement graph G′=(V,Ec)G^{\prime}=(V,E^{c}), and moreover, the smallest clique cover corresponds to the chromatic number of the complement graph. Thus the previous construction suffices.

A.5 Permutation Mixers

In this section, we consider problems with QAOA mappings that use the mixers of Section 5 for domains consisting of ordering, permutations, or schedules. In the SMS problems below, for simplicity, we take all time parameters to be nonnegative integers.

A.5.1 TravelingSalespersonProblem (TSP) [Section 5.1]

Problem: Given a set of nn cities and distances d:[n]2→ℝ+d:{[n]}^{2}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{+}, find an ordering of the cities that minimizes the total distance traveled on the corresponding tour.
Approximability: NPO-complete [86]. MetricTSP is APX-complete [87] and has a 3/23/2-approximation [88]. The corresponding MaxTSP problem is approximable within 7/57/5 for symmetric distance, and 63/3863/38 if asymmetric.
Configuration space and domain: Orderings of the cities {𝜾}\{\boldsymbol{\iota}\}.
Objective: min f⁡(𝜾)=∑j=1ndιj,ιj+1f(\boldsymbol{\iota})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}d_{\iota_{j},\iota_{j+1}}.
Partial mixer: Partial permutation swap mixer.
Encoding: Direct one-hot.
Compilation:

  • •

    Phase separator: HP(enc)=∑i=1n∑u=1n∑v=1nd⁡(u,v)​Zu,i​Zv,i+1H_{\mathrm{P}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{u=1}^{n}\sum_{v=1}^{n}d(u,v)Z_{u,i}Z_{v,i+1}.

  • •

    Partial mixer: UPS,{i,j},{u,v}(enc)​(β)=e−i​β​HPS,{i,j},{u,v}U_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}(\beta)=e^{-i\beta H_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}}, where HPS,{i,j},{u,v}(enc)H_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}^{(\mathrm{enc})} is given in Equation (55).

Initial state: Arbitrary ordering.
Resource count:

  • •

    Color-parity permutation swap mixer (Section 5.1): At most (n−1)​(n2)(n-1)\binom{n}{2} 44-qubit partial mixers, in depth at most 2​n2n.

  • •

    Phase separator: n2​(n−1)n^{2}(n-1) mutually commuting two-qubit gates. Depth no more than DG+1D_{G}+1.

  • •

    Initial state: nn single-qubit XX gates. Depth 11.

A.5.2 SMS, Minimizing Total Weighted Squared Tardiness [Section 5.2]

Problem: (1​|dj|​∑wj​Tj2)(1|d_{j}|\sum w_{j}T_{j}^{2}). Given a set of jobs with processing times 𝐩\mathbf{p}, deadlines 𝐝∈ℤ+\mathbf{d}\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}, and weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}, find a schedule that minimizes the total weighted squared tardiness ∑j=1nwj​Tj2\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}T_{j}^{2}.
Approximability: Considered in Reference [89].
Configuration space and domain: Orderings of the jobs {𝐢}\{\mathbf{i}\}, and an integer slack variable yj∈[0,dj−pj]y_{j}\in[0,d_{j}-p_{j}] for each job.
Objective: min f⁡(𝜾,𝐲)=∑j=1nwj​(sj​(𝜾)+pj−dj+yj)2.f(\boldsymbol{\iota},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}{\left(s_{j}(\boldsymbol{\iota})+p_{j}-d_{j}+y_{j}\right)}^{2}.
Partial mixer: Partial permutation swap mixer for computational qubits; binary mixer mixer for the slack qubits.
Encoding: Direct one-hot for the ordering variables; binary for the slack variables.
Compilation:

  • •

    Phase separator: The encoded phase separator is a 3-local Hamiltonian containing

    • –

      all 1-local terms;

    • –

      all 2-local terms of two computational qubits corresponding to different jobs at different places in the ordering, all 2-local terms of two ancilla qubits corresponding to the same job, and all 2-local terms of one computational qubit and one ancilla qubit except when they correspond to different jobs and the computational qubit corresponds to that job being last in the ordering;

    • –

      all 3-local terms of three computational qubits corresponding to different jobs at different places in the ordering and all 3-local terms containing two computational qubits corresponding to different jobs at different places in the ordering and one ancilla qubit corresponding to the later job.

  • •

    Partial mixer: HPS,{i,j},{u,v}(enc)=Su,i+​Sv,j+​Su,j−​Sv,i−+Su,i−​Sv,j−​Su,j+​Sv,i+H_{\mathrm{PS},{\{i,j\},\{u,v\}}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=S^{+}_{u,i}S^{+}_{v,j}S^{-}_{u,j}S^{-}_{v,i}+S^{-}_{u,i}S^{-}_{v,j}S^{+}_{u,j}S^{+}_{v,i}.

  • •

    Initial state Arbitrary ordering.

Resource count:

  • •

    Color-parity permutation swap mixer (Section 5.1): At most (n−1)​(n2)(n-1)\binom{n}{2} 44-qubit partial mixers, in depth at most 2​n2n. Single-qubit XX mixer for slack binary variables can be done in parallel with the permutation swap mixer.

  • •

    Phase separator: Let μi=⌈log2⁡(di−pi+1)⌉\mu_{i}=\left\lceil\log_{2}(d_{i}-p_{i}+1)\right\rceil be the number of bits needed for the slack variable yiy_{i}, and μ=∑i=1nμi\mu=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{i}.

    • –

      Number of 1-local gates: n2+μn^{2}+\mu.

    • –

      Number of 2-local gates: 2​(n2)2+∑i=1n(μi2)+μ⁡(n2−n+1)2{\binom{n}{2}}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{\mu_{i}}{2}+\mu(n^{2}-n+1).

    • –

      Number of 3-local gates: 6​(n3)2+2​μ​(n2)26{\binom{n}{3}}^{2}+2\mu{\binom{n}{2}}^{2}.

  • •

    Initial state: nn single-qubit XX gates. Depth 11.

A.5.3 SMS, Minimizing Total Weighted Tardiness [Section 5.3]

Problem: (1​|dj|​∑wj​Tj)(1|d_{j}|\sum w_{j}T_{j}). Given a set of nn jobs with processing times 𝐩\mathbf{p}, deadlines 𝐝∈ℤ+\mathbf{d}\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}, and weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}, find a schedule that minimizes the total weighted tardiness ∑j=1nwj​Tj\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}T_{j}.
Approximability: There exists an (n−1)(n-1)-approximation [90]. The decision version is strongly NP-hard [91].
Configuration space and domain: Orderings of the jobs {𝐢}\{\mathbf{i}\}.
Objective: f⁡(𝜾)=∑i=1nwi​max⁡{0,di−si​(𝜾)−pi}.f(\boldsymbol{\iota})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\max\{0,d_{i}-s_{i}(\boldsymbol{\iota})-p_{i}\}.
Encoding: Absolute one-hot.
Mixing rule: Swap two jobs only if they are scheduled in consecutive order.
Partial mixer: Partial time-swap mixer (specific to the absolute encoding).
Initial state: Arbitrary ordering.
Compilation:

  • •

    Phase separator: HP(enc)=∑i=1nwi​∑t=di−pi+1hi(t+pi−di)​Zi,t.H_{\mathrm{P}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\sum_{t=d_{i}-p_{i}+1}^{h_{i}}(t+p_{i}-d_{i})Z_{i,t}.

  • •

    Partial mixer: HTS,t,{i,j}(enc)=Si,t+pj+​Sj,t+​Si,t−​Sj,t+pi−+Si,t+pj−​Sj,t−.Si,t+​Sj,t+pi+{H_{\mathrm{TS},{t,\{i,j\}}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=S^{+}_{i,t+p_{j}}S^{+}_{j,t}S^{-}_{i,t}S^{-}_{j,t+p_{i}}+S^{-}_{i,t+p_{j}}S^{-}_{j,t}.S^{+}_{i,t}S^{+}_{j,t+p_{i}}}.

Resource count:

  • •

    Color–time partitioned time-swap mixer: h​(n2)h\binom{n}{2} 4-qubit gates in depth h​κh\kappa.

  • •

    Phase separator: At most n​hnh single-qubit gates, depth 1.

  • •

    Initial state: nn single-qubit XX gates, depth 11.

A.5.4 SMS, with Release Dates [Section 5.4]

Problem: (1|dj,rj|f)(1|d_{j},r_{j}|f). Given a set of jobs with processing times 𝐩\mathbf{p}, deadlines 𝐝\mathbf{d}, release times 𝐫∈ℤ+\mathbf{r}\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} and weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}, find a schedule that minimizes some (given) function ff of the schedule, e.g., weighted total tardiness such that each job starts no earlier than its release time.
Approximability: For all deadlines being zero, the minimal weighted total tardiness (completion times in this special case) is 1.6851.685-approximable [92].
Configuration space: {𝐬}=×j=1n[Wj∪{bj}]\{\mathbf{s}\}=\times_{j=1}^{n}\left[W_{j}\cup\{b_{j}\}\right], where Wj=[rj,h−pj]W_{j}=[r_{j},h-p_{j}] is the window of times in which job jj can start and bjb_{j} is the job’s “buffer” slot.
Domain: Schedules in the configuration space such that no two jobs overlap.
Objective: Maximize (or minimize) a given cost function f⁡(𝐬)f(\mathbf{s}), e.g., weighted total tardiness f⁡(𝐬)=∑j=1nwj​Tjf(\mathbf{s})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}T_{j}, where Tj=max⁡{0,di−si−pi}T_{j}=\max\{0,d_{i}-s_{i}-p_{i}\} is the tardiness of job jj.
Mixing rule: Swap a job between time t∈ht\in h and its buffer slot if no other job is running at time tt.
Partial mixer: Controlled null-swap mixer; see Section 5.4.
Initial state: Greedy earliest-release-date schedule.
Encoding: One-hot encoding.
Compilation:

  • •

    Partial mixer: HNS,i,t(enc)=(∏j≠i∏t′∈nbhdi,t​(j)12​(I+Zj,t′))​(Xi,t​Xi,bi+Yi,t​Yi,bi).H_{\mathrm{NS},{i,t}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=\left(\prod_{j\neq i}\prod_{t^{\prime}\in\mathrm{nbhd}_{i,t}(j)}\frac{1}{2}(I+Z_{j,t^{\prime}})\right)\left(X_{i,t}X_{i,b_{i}}+Y_{i,t}Y_{i,b_{i}}\right).

  • •

    Phase separator (for min weighted total tardiness): See Equation (77).

Resource count:

  • •

    Controlled null-swap mixer: SMS-instance dependent, see discussion in Section 5.4.

  • •

    Phase separator (for min weighted total tardiness): At most ∑j(h−dj+1)\sum_{j}(h-d_{j}+1) single-qubit ZZ gates. Depth 11.

  • •

    Initial state: nn single-qubit XX gates. Depth 11.

Appendix B Glossary of Mapping Terms

Here, we provide a summary the mapping terminology that appears throughout the paper.

B.1 Mixers

We list partial mixers by mixing mechanism in Appendix B.1.1, and by different ways to partition, used for partitioned mixers, in Appendix B.1.2

B.1.1 Partial Mixing Hamiltonians

For strings and subsets thereof, we focus on mixing operators that are composed of operators acting independently on each of the variables. Specifically, we consider the following single-qudit mixing operators in the absence of constraints:

  • •

    rr-nearby-values mixer: Hr​-​NV=∑a=1r(X˘a+(X˘†)a)H_{r\text{-}\mathrm{NV}}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}\left({\breve{X}}^{a}+{({\breve{X}}^{\dagger})}^{a}\right). The special cases of r=1r=1 and r=d−1r=d-1 are called the “ring mixer” and “fully-connected mixer”, respectively.

  • •

    simple binary mixer: When d=2ld=2^{l} is a power of two: Hbinary(enc)=∑i=1lXi.H_{\mathrm{binary}}^{(\mathrm{enc})}=\sum_{i=1}^{l}X_{i}.

  • •

    null-swap mixer: For cases when one of the dd values corresponds to a “null” value (e.g., black or uncolored in graph coloring), HNS=∑a=1d−1(|0⟩​⟨a|+|a⟩​⟨0|)H_{\mathrm{NS}}=\sum_{a=1}^{d-1}\left(\ket{0}\bra{a}+\ket{a}\bra{0}\right).

For problems in the ordering/schedules family, we considered swapping-based mixers.

  • •

    Value-selective permutation swap mixer: Swaps the iith and jjth elements in the ordering if those elements are uu and vv, see Equation (46) in Section 5.1.

  • •

    Value-independent permutation swap mixer: Swaps the iith and jjth elements of the ordering regardless of which items those are, see Equation (48) in Section 5.1.

When there are constraints, we considered modifications of the above mixers that are controlled on not violating the constraints. A few examples:

  • •

    Controlled null-swap mixer:

    • –

      Section 4.3 for MaxColorableInducedSubgraph, Equation (27).

    • –

      Section 5.4 for SMS with release dates, Equation (73).

  • •

    Controlled-SWAP mixer: Section 4.4 for MinGraphColoring, Equation (34).

B.1.2 Partitions

The two elementary partitions we use for generating the family of partitioned mixing unitaries are:

  • •

    Parity-mixer: For Hamiltonian terms of type ∑uAu​Bu+1\sum_{u}A_{u}B_{u+1}, where u∈[n]u\in[n] and AuA_{u} and Bu+1B_{u+1} are operators acting on qubit uu and u+1u+1, respectively. Partition the index set {u}\{u\} into even and odd subsets. See Section 4.1 for details.

  • •

    Color-mixer: For index pairs (u,v)∈([n]2)(u,v)\in{[n]\choose 2}, let 𝒫col=(P1,…,Pκ)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{col}}=(P_{1},\ldots,P_{\kappa}) be an ordered partition of the indices ([n]2)\binom{[n]}{2} into κ\kappa parts such that each part contains only mutually disjoint pairs of indices from [n][n]. This is equivalent to considering a κ\kappa-edge-coloring of the complete graph KnK_{n}, and assigning an ordering to the colors, so we call 𝒫col\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{col}} the “color partition”. For even nn, κ=n−1\kappa=n-1 suffices, and for odd nn, κ=n\kappa=n. See Section 5.1 for its use.

For mixing Hamiltonians of different coupling connectivity, these partitions can be combined and tailored as desired. For example, the color-parity permutation swap mixer for TSP in Section 5.1 and the time–color partition for SMS (1​|dj|​∑wj​Tj)(1|d_{j}|\sum w_{j}T_{j}) in Section 5.3.

B.2 Encodings

We considered two types of encodings of strings into qubit space. One-hot encoding enables more concise circuits at the expense of requiring more qubits, whereas binary encoding makes the opposite trade-off.

  • •

    One-hot encoding: The qudit basis states |a⟩\ket{a}, a=0,…,d−1a=0,\dots,d-1, are encoded as the dd-qubit states |0⟩⊗a⊗|1⟩⊗|1⟩⊗d−1−a{\ket{0}}^{\otimes a}\otimes\ket{1}\otimes\ket{1}^{\otimes{d-1-a}}. See Section 4.1.1

  • •

    Binary encoding: Each qudit basis state |a⟩\ket{a} is encoded as the ℓ\ell-qubit basis state |a2⟩\ket{a_{2}}, where a2a_{2} denotes the binary representation of aa, and ℓ=⌈log2⁡d⌉\ell=\lceil\log_{2}d\rceil. See Section 4.1.1.

    A generalization of the binary encoding is radix encoding, which represents aa in base-rr, with positive integer rr. While the binary encoding is convenient for qubits, and is hence appealing in terms of implementability, it is plausible that for some problems, a more general radix encoding could be a natural choice.

For problems in the ordering/scheduling family, the encoding is composed of two-steps: First encoding into strings, and then applying the above encodings into qubit space. The following encodings are considered for step one:

  • •

    Direct encoding: An ordering 𝜾=(ι1,…,ιn)\boldsymbol{\iota}=\left(\iota_{1},\ldots,\iota_{n}\right) is encoded directly as a string [n]n{[n]}^{n} of integers. It is demonstrated for TSP and SMS (1​|dj|​∑jwj​Tj2)(1|d_{j}|\sum_{j}w_{j}T^{2}_{j}) in Sections 5.1 and 5.2, respectively.

  • •

    Absolute encoding: To encode the ordering 𝜾=(ι1,…,ιn)\boldsymbol{\iota}=(\iota_{1},\ldots,\iota_{n}), we assigned each item ii a value si∈[0,h]s_{i}\in[0,h], where the “horizon” hh is a parameter of the encodings, such that for all i<ji<j, sιi<sιjs_{\iota_{i}}<s_{\iota_{j}}. It is demonstrated for SMS (1​|dj|​∑jwj​Tj)(1|d_{j}|\sum_{j}w_{j}T_{j}) in Section 5.3.

The name of the overall encoding indicates both steps. For example:

  • •

    Direct one-hot encoding, see Section 5.1.

  • •

    Absolute one-hot encoding, see Section 5.3.

Appendix C Elementary Operators

Here, we elaborate on some of the basic quantum operators used in the text and their properties. Appendix C.1 explains the relationship between the SWAP\mathrm{SWAP} gate and the XY-model Hamiltonian, which were each used as building blocks for encoded mixers in many mappings. Appendix C.2 contains a brief review of generalized Pauli operators for qudits of arbitrary dimension.

C.1 SWAP and XY Opertors

We examined the relationship between the quantum SWAP operator SWAPi,j\mathrm{SWAP}_{i,j}, which swaps the state of qubit ii and jj, and the XY operator, 12​(Xi​Xj+Yi​Yj)\frac{1}{2}(X_{i}X_{j}+Y_{i}Y_{j}). In many of our mapping constructions, these operators can be used interchangeably; an exception is given in the last item below.

Recall Equation (10) and the discussion of SWAP preceeding it. The XY operator acting on qubits i,ji,j can be similarly expressed as:

X​Yi,j:=12​(Xi​Xj+Yi​Yj)=|1i​0j⟩​⟨0i​1j|+|0i​1j⟩​⟨1i​0j|.XY_{i,j}:=\frac{1}{2}(X_{i}X_{j}+Y_{i}Y_{j})=\ket{1_{i}0_{j}}\!\bra{0_{i}1_{j}}+\ket{0_{i}1_{j}}\!\bra{1_{i}0_{j}}. (79)

We observed the following connections between the two operators:

  • •

    In the subspace spanned by {|01⟩,|10⟩}\{\ket{01},\ket{10}\}, X​Yi,jXY_{i,j} and SWAPi,j\mathrm{SWAP}_{i,j} behave identically.

  • •

    In the subspace {|11⟩,|00⟩}\{\ket{11},\ket{00}\}, X​Yi,jXY_{i,j} acts as null while SWAPi,j\mathrm{SWAP}_{i,j} acts as an identity.

  • •

    The operators X​Yi,jXY_{i,j} and SWAPi,j\mathrm{SWAP}_{i,j} are both Hermitian. SWAPi,j\mathrm{SWAP}_{i,j} is unitary.

  • •

    Applied to a multiqubit system, Hamiltonians of the form HSWAP=∑i,jSWAPi,jH_{\mathrm{SWAP}}=\sum_{i,j}\mathrm{SWAP}_{i,j} or HXY=∑i,jX​Yi,jH_{\text{XY}}=\sum_{i,j}XY_{i,j}, where either sum may be taken over arbitrary subsets of indices, each preserve the Hamming weight of computational basis states; hence, so do the corresponding unitaries exp⁡[−i​β​HXY]\exp[-i\beta H_{\text{XY}}] and exp⁡[−i​β​HSWAP]\exp[-i\beta H_{\mathrm{SWAP}}]. Although the two operators do not behave identically on the full Hilbert space, they can both serve as mixers in situations in which Hamming weight is the relevant constraint.

  • •

    To enforce simultaneous swaps of multiple qubit pairs, in Hamiltonians such as H=∏{i,j}SWAPi,jH=\prod_{\{i,j\}}\mathrm{SWAP}_{i,j}, each SWAPi,j\mathrm{SWAP}_{i,j} cannot in general be directly replaced by X​Yi,jXY_{i,j} due to the second item above. See the TSP problem in Section 5.1 as an example.

C.2 Generalized Pauli Gates for Qudits

Consider dd-dimensional qudits. Let ω=e2​π​i/d\omega=e^{2\pi i/d}. Define the operators:

Z˘\displaystyle{\breve{Z}} =∑a=0d−1ωda​|a⟩​⟨a|,\displaystyle=\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}\omega_{d}^{a}\ket{a}\bra{a}, X˘\displaystyle{\breve{X}} =∑a=0d−1|a+1⟩​⟨a|,\displaystyle=\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}\ket{a+1}\bra{a}, (80)

where all arithmetic is modulo dd. As in the main text, we used operator notations “Z˘{\breve{Z}}” and “X˘{\breve{X}}” for qudits of arbitrary dimension, and reserved “XX” and “ZZ” specifically for the qubit case. For d=2d=2, they are the same. Note that for d>2d>2, the generalized Pauli operators, while unitary, are not Hermitian. In many cases, we used the sum of a generalized Pauli operator and its conjugate to generalize its qubit analog, e.g., X˘+X˘†{\breve{X}}+{\breve{X}}^{\dagger} to generalize XX.

Because X˘r=∑a=0d−1|a+r⟩​⟨a|{\breve{X}}^{r}=\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}\ket{a+r}\!\bra{a}, it and its Hermitian conjugate X˘r+(X˘†)r{\breve{X}}^{r}+{({\breve{X}}^{\dagger})}^{r} together generate transitions between |a⟩\ket{a} and |a+r⟩\ket{a+r} for any aa. Section 4.1.1 uses this operator in the coloring of a single vertex.
